quick.summary: Why memory warnings should not wake you up at night, and what to alert on instead.
quick.takeaway: Only wake humans for alerts that cause real pain to the users.

beats.line: My phone rang at three for a memory warning.
But nothing was actually broken. Why wake a human for that?
Imagine a smoke alarm in a busy restaurant kitchen.
If it rings every time a pan gets hot, you ignore it.
Right, you only want it to ring for a real fire.
Exactly. Pages should only happen when someone is really hurting.
We call this symptom based alerting.
Can I just say alert on pain?
You can. No user pain means no waking up.
So a memory warning is just a ticket for the morning.
Exactly. Let the machines track warnings. Save humans for fires.

quiz.question: Which warning should actually trigger a page to wake an engineer?
options: A failed checkout page preventing users from buying.
High memory use on a background server.
A processor running hot for five minutes.
quiz.explanation: Pages are for fires. A broken checkout hurts users right now, while the others are just early warnings.

quiz.question: An alert on pain means we ignore underlying server warnings entirely.
quiz.explanation: We do not ignore warnings, we just let computers log them or create tickets instead of waking humans up.
